RoboLearn · Isaac Lab · Recorded implementation comparison

Cartpole FlashSAC: learning and runtime in Torch and Warp

The authors’ architecture across eager Torch, compiled Torch, compiled mixed precision, and captured Warp FP32, evaluated on the same Cartpole MDP.

12 recorded runs · 4,915,200 collected transitions per run · final requested iteration 200
OverviewLearning curves Final evaluationsRuntimeOptimizer health MethodsEvidence

Comparison scope

This experiment asks whether the faithful Warp FlashSAC port learns a useful policy and how its production cost compares with three Torch recipes. Quality comes from common evaluations, and speed comes from measured training phases. Numerical trajectories may differ across implementations and precisions.

In the complete recorded cohort, final iteration 200 means were Torch FP32 · eager: return 0.988, upright 43.5% (observed seed range 7.7%–85.9%), cart-bound survival 20.8% (n=3); Torch FP32 · compiled: return 2.67, upright 65.4% (observed seed range 7.1%–96.4%), cart-bound survival 66.1% (n=3); Torch FP16 AMP · compiled: return 3.78, upright 82.4% (observed seed range 71.2%–94.9%), cart-bound survival 69.0% (n=3); Warp FP32 · captured: return 0.986, upright 39.8% (observed seed range 8.9%–96.1%), cart-bound survival 33.3% (n=3). All included runs collected 4,915,200 transitions; runtime is compared at that fixed sample budget. Warp’s mean warmed throughput (n=3) was 0.209× Torch FP32 · compiled (n=3) and 0.206× Torch FP16 AMP · compiled (n=3). Mean full training-process wall was 445 s for Warp (n=3), versus Torch FP32 · compiled 1.09e+03 s (Torch/Warp wall ratio 2.447; n=3); Torch FP16 AMP · compiled 557 s (Torch/Warp wall ratio 1.253; n=3).

12/12 runs contain all requested evaluations. The four-recipe, three-seed cohort is complete.
Torch FP32 · eager: seeds 0, 1, 2; Torch FP32 · compiled: seeds 0, 1, 2; Torch FP16 AMP · compiled: seeds 0, 1, 2; Warp FP32 · captured: seeds 0, 1, 2

No universal speed or learning advantage follows from this cohort. Three seeds support descriptive means and observed ranges, not a statistical significance claim.

Survival and time-limit completion measure episode termination. Falling or rotating the pole does not terminate this MDP. The native joint_pos_target_l2 reward penalizes the squared pole angle wrapped to [−π, π], and the angle RMS shown here uses the same wrapping. Policy observations retain raw angles; unwrapped_pole_angle_squared_mean is a rotation diagnostic. Native return also includes velocity and termination penalties.

Production-process wall time, measured training loop time, and first-use compile/capture costs answer different questions. The process does not include OSMO queueing, image preparation, artifact retrieval, or unrelated jobs. Production process time is the training subprocess; the separate common evaluation subprocess is retained in raw evidence. Loop totals and the learning-curve time axis use synchronized collection-plus-update iteration wall time; collection/update phase measurements also use CUDA events. Learn wall time includes prepare, logging, and native checkpoint I/O; checkpoint totals also include the explicit final save. The exact measurement boundaries are retained below. Shared GPU measurements must not be described as isolated unless their runtime evidence explicitly establishes isolation.

Completed optimizer work and native-state health

Attempted replay updates can differ from completed Adam steps when AMP skips a nonfinite gradient. Parameter-step minima/maxima and coverage expose incomplete optimizer state. Health comes from native checkpoints, not from training return alone.

Method and interpretation

  • Common task: the existing Isaac Lab Cartpole MDP is shared by all recipes. Physics uses the configured backend; observations, rewards, resets, and terminations remain Torch operations. Physics and the Warp learner use separate graphs. This is not one fully Warp environment-and-learning graph.
  • Budget: 1024 environments, 24 vector steps per iteration, and 200 requested iterations. Checkpoints: [0, 50, 100, 150, 200]. Warmup transitions count toward the production transition budget; evaluation transitions do not.
  • Cartpole semantics: control interval 1/60 s (physics step 1/120 s, decimation 2), 300-step / 5-second time limit, and cart-bound termination at ±3 m. There is no pole-fall termination. Native rewards integrate the control-step dt; the alive-only return upper bound is 5 over a 5-second episode. Upright occupancy uses |wrapped angle| < 0.25 rad. Evaluation measures each world’s first episode after a common reset, and aggregates episode-normalized state metrics. Survival and time-limit completion identify the same event here. Action saturation is the fraction of normalized actions with magnitude > 0.95, averaged over actions and first episodes; it describes control behavior without defining a quality gate. One unscored native reset initializes the actuator soft velocity-limit buffers before the scored seeded resets; per-run initialization receipts retain the before/after limits.
  • Policy comparison: the four recipes use the authors’ actor, twin distributional critic, normalizations, bounded stochastic actions, and replay update schedule. Common initial parameter fixtures and evaluation initial-state hashes are retained for inspection. Evaluations use deterministic policy actions, 128 worlds, and reset seed 10000. Different RNG and FP32/FP16 arithmetic can produce different learned policies; matching every Torch update is not required. One common 128-world reset fixture provides paired evaluations, and limits evidence for generalization to other resets or environment conditions.
  • Scope: this controlled Cartpole implementation comparison is not a reproduction of the FlashSAC paper’s robot results. Training-return windows may differ; common evaluations are the quality comparison.
  • Artifact-transfer overlap: transfer began at 2026-10-09T17:38:28.204386Z with 8 runs completed, and ended at 2026-10-09T18:22:44.034348Z. Network and disk artifact-transfer traffic overlapped later training runs. The transfer ran no GPU profiling or computation; host or disk overhead may affect later timings. Recorded timing values are unchanged. Staged bytes describe retained files, not measured wire traffic.
